sections.overview: The Australian pelican is a large, mobile waterbird widespread across Australia, New Guinea and western Indonesia, with occasional records farther into the Pacific.
sections.identification: It is mostly white with black wings and a massive pink bill and throat pouch; males are larger, with bills around 40–50 centimetres long.
sections.habitat: It uses inland and coastal open waters, including lakes, rivers, estuaries, swamps and lagoons, moving widely as water and food availability change.
sections.diet: Fish form most of its diet, though it also takes crustaceans and other aquatic prey; the pouch works as a short-term scoop net, not a food-storage bag.
sections.behavior: It often fishes cooperatively, herding fish into shallow or confined water before scooping them up; individuals can also forage alone.
sections.reproduction: Breeding may occur at different times and depends strongly on rainfall; pairs nest colonially on islands or secluded shores and share incubation.
sections.ecology: It is the only pelican native to Australia and is highly nomadic, travelling long distances between wetlands.
sections.conservation: It remains widespread, but breeding success and food supply depend on changing wetland conditions; the sources consulted do not establish a current population trend.
